## Abstract

The effect of cold forging on the microstructure and corrosion behavior of 316L

stainless steel (SS) in molten salt was investigated.  Static corrosion experiments were

performed in FLiNaK (LiF-NaF-KF: 46.5-11.5-42 mol.%) at 600 oC for 50 hours in a

glove box.  The results show that cold forging gives rise to enhanced corrosion of 316L

SS in molten fluoride salt due to the increase of crystallographic defects.  Based on the

potentiodynamic polarization results, the corrosion rate of 50% reduced cold-forged

316L SS is about 2.1 times larger than that of the as-received 316L SS in molten

FLiNaK salt at 600 oC.

Keywords: Molten salt, 316L stainless steel, Cold forging, High-temperature corrosion

## 1. Introduction

Fission reactors are a type of nuclear reactor that generate energy through the

process of nuclear fission. Generation IV reactors are the next generation of nuclear

fission reactors that are being developed to address the limitations of current nuclear

technology while enhancing safety, sustainability, efficiency and economics [1].

Among the Generation IV reactors, molten salt reactors (MSRs) potentially have the

greatest inherent safety and have received more and more attention in recent years [2].

In MSRs, the primary coolants are molten salts.  These molten salts are characterized

by low melting points, high volumetric heat capacities, high boiling points, low vapor

pressure, etc [3-5].  The MSR can operate at or close to atmospheric pressure even

running at high temperature (e.g. 700 oC) for a greater thermal efficiency [5] and

reduced probability of pressure boundary penetration accidents.  However, molten salts

are naturally corrosive at high temperatures, especially when the salt is not purified

[5,6].  Performance of structural materials corrosion in molten salt needs to be

understood so that economic and safety decisions can be made with greater certainty in

the development of MSR [3,7].

316L stainless steel (SS) is a Fe-Ni-Cr austenitic stainless steel and offers high

temperature creep strength, high yield and tensile strengths, as well as excellent

oxidation resistance at high temperatures [8,9].  Additionally, 316L SS also exhibits

excellent resistance to radiation damage and has been extensively used in the nuclear

industry [10-12].  Corrosion experiments performed in Oak Ridge National Laboratory

(ORNL) in a thermal-convection loop revealed that the corrosion rate of 316 SS was

correlated with the impurities contents of the molten salt and showed an acceptable

corrosion resistance in purified molten fluoride salts [13,14].  Due to the above reasons,

316L SS was chosen as a candidate structural material for the MSR systems.  316L SS

contains 16-18 wt.% Cr and derives its high corrosion resistance in conventional

environments (e.g. high-temperature aqueous) from the formation of a compact and

stable barrier layer of the passive film on the surface of the material [15].  However,

different from the conventional hot corrosion, the passive film formed on 316L SS is

soluble in high temperature molten fluoride salt and is therefore unprotective [6,16].

Corrosion of 316L SS is an unavoidable issue for its application in MSR systems.

Cold forging is an economic, production efficient, and reliable process to improve

the yield, tensile strength and fatigue resistance of alloys [17,18].  316L SS, with a

carbon content of less than 0.05wt.%, has good ductility and is appropriate to use cold

forging to improve its mechanical properties [19].  The cold-forged 316L SS can be

utilized if 316L SS is chosen as a structural material for MSR.  However, studies

confirmed that cold-work affects the corrosion resistance of stainless steels [20-22].

For example, Meng et al. [23] revealed that austenitic stainless steels have much higher

stress corrosion cracking (SCC) susceptibility than the annealed materials in simulated

power water reactor environments.  Chen et al. [24] studied the SCC behavior of Alloy

690 with different degrees of cold work in supercritical water environment and found

that the SCC and creep CGRs increased with degrees of cold work.  Saez-Maderuelo et

al. [25] reported that cold worked 316L is susceptible to SCC in supercritical water

reactor conditions where the susceptibility of this alloy increases with temperature.  The

prior plastic deformation of 316L SS increased its susceptibility to environmental

cracking in SCW.  The effect of cold forging on the corrosion of steels has been

extensively investigated for pressurized water reactors.  However, to our knowledge,

the effect of cold forging on the corrosion behavior of 316L stainless steel in high

temperature molten fluoride salts has been less studied and therefore additional studies

are necessary for its application in molten salt environments.

In our previous work [26], we evaluated the relationship between degree of cold

forging and the materials corrosion behavior, and found that the corrosion behavior of

50% cold-forged 316 SS shows is different from lower cold forging samples (5-30%).

Samples with lower cold forging samples (5-30%) showed more IGC, while the 50 %

cold forging sample had less IGC but the shallowest corrosion depth. However, it

remains uncertain whether the corrosion resistance of the 50 % cold forging sample

improved. The excessive CF levels sample resulted in a decrease in corrosion depth,

while it may increase an overall corrosion quantity due to general corrosion rather than

IGC. In order to provide insights into the effect of higher cold forging 316L SS and

quantify the corrosion rates in molten salt. In this work, static corrosion experiments of

## 2. Experimental

2.1. Materials

Two coupons of type 316L SS with dimensions of 10 mm × 8 mm × 2 mm were

used in this study, and the chemical composition is shown in Table 1.  One coupon was

kept in the as-received condition for comparison, and the other one was cold-forged to

50% reduction in plate thickness.  Prior to the static corrosion experiments, the samples

were ground down to 2000 grit with SiC paper.  After that, all the samples were

ultrasonically cleaned with deionized water and acetone, and then dried and kept in an

argon gas glove box to maintain an inert atmosphere and prevent oxidation before the

corrosion experiments.

To minimize the effect of impurities on the corrosion behavior (as impurities are

highly corrosive and can react with steel matrix and affects the quantify analysis results)

[5], we used high-purity eutectic FLiNaK salt (46.5 mol.% LiF-11.5 mol.% NaF-42

mol.% KF) in this study, which was supplied by Oak Ridge National Laboratory, USA.

As is known that the corrosion rate of alloys in purified FLiNaK salt is very slow [4].

To investigate and highlight the corrosion behavior differences between these two

coupons, we added FeF3, a typical metal fluoride in MSR system, to the FLiNaK salt

as an oxidant to accelerate the corrosion of 316L SS in the melt.

2.2. Static corrosion experiments

To prevent the galvanic corrosion driven by dissimilar materials, a 25 mm diameter

cylinder of 316L SS stock material was used to machine the corrosion crucible.  The

crucible was partitioned with several 9 mm diameter cylindrical capsules, and the

schematic of the crucible is shown in Fig. 1.  After machining, the steel crucible was

ultrasonically cleaned with deionized water and alcohol successively.  Finally, the

crucible was dried and transferred into an argon gas glove box.

Subsequently, 0.9 g FLiNaK salt and 75 mg FeF3 powder were mixed and loaded

into each cylindrical capsule, and then was heated to 600 oC to melt the salt in the glove

box.  After the salt was melted, one coupon was dropped into each crucible capsule for

the static corrosion experiments.   The moisture and oxygen contents in the glove box

were both below 1ppm during the corrosion experiment.  After 50 h exposure in the

FLiNaK salt, the samples were retrieved and cooled in the glove box for subsequent

analysis.

2.3. Potentiodynamic polarization

Potentiodynamic polarization experiments were carried out to evaluate the

corrosion rate of the 316L SS and cold-forged 316L SS in molten FLiNaK salt.  A three

electrodes electrochemical system was used in this study.  A graphite rod with a

diameter of 5 mm and a Pt wire were employed as counter electrode (CE) and reference

electrode (RE), respectively.  Two coupons (one as-received 316L SS and one cold-

forged 316L SS) with dimensions of 50 mm × 6 mm × 2 mm were used as working

electrode (WE) for the polarization measurements.  Prior to the experiments, the two

coupons were ground down to 2000 grit with SiC paper and then cleaned in deionized

water and acetone.  After that, one end of the coupon was connected to a 316L SS wire

using a steel sleeve connector to prepare the WE for experiments.  To avoid repetition

and save space, details of the electrochemical experiments can be found in our previous

work [27].

After the FLiNaK salt was heated to 600 oC, the electrodes were dipped

approximately 15 mm into the melt under the atmosphere of argon to begin the

experiments.  Potentiodynamic polarization measurement was carried out after the

electrodes were placed in the salt for 1 h to reach a quasi-static open circuit potential

(OCP).  The scan rate of the potentiodynamic polarization measurement is 0.5 mV·s−1.

2.4. Materials characterization

After completing the static corrosion experiments, the samples were taken out from

the glove box and cleaned with deionized water and ethanol to remove the residual

FLiNaK salt.  After that, the samples were cut and mounted in epoxy resin for cross-

sectional examination.  The chemical compositions and structures of the samples were

examined using optical microscopy (OM) and EBSD.  The corrosion morphologies and

elemental distributions of the samples were characterized using an FEI Quanta 3D FEG

SEM and EDS.  To reveal the grain boundaries of the samples for OM analysis, the

polished samples were electro-etched in 50% HNO3 solution at 1.5 V for 1 min.  The

cross-sectional samples were ground with silicon carbide papers down to 2500 grit and

then polished with 0.05 μm alumina slurry.  For the EBSD samples, an additional

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Effect of cold forging on microstructure

In order to study the effect of cold forging on the grain microstructures, these two

samples were polished and electro-etched in 50% HNO3 solution at 1.5 V for 1 min.

and then observed using OM.  As shown in Fig. 2, cold forging has a significant impact

on the microstructure of the material. From Fig. 2(a) and 2(b), the 316L SS before cold

forging mainly exhibits an equiaxed grain structure without apparent orientation.

However, after cold forging, the surface grains of the material become noticeably larger,

while the grains in the cross-section become significantly smaller, and the characteristic

crystal orientation caused by the cold forging begins to appear (Fig. 2(c) and 2(d)). This

change indicates that the cold forging process plays an important role in the

rearrangement of the crystal structure and the variation in grain size. During the cold

forging process, the 316L SS undergoes plastic deformation under applied stress,

leading to an increase in dislocation density within the lattice, which promotes grain

refinement and the formation of orientation, which agrees well with the literatures that

the cold working leads to internal dislocations, deformation zones and grain refinement

[28-30].

### 3.2 Corrosion behavior

*Fig. 6 shows the surface and cross-sectional SEM micrographs of the pristine*

316L SS after exposure in molten FLiNaK salt at 600 oC for 50 h.  The surface

morphology in Fig. 6(a) displayed an even corrosion surface with minor attack to grain

boundaries, although such form of corrosion attack was not extensive as revealed by

the cross-sectional micrograph in Fig. 6(b).  Only slight depletion of near-surface Cr

was observed from Fig. 6(c).  It is well known that the main corrosion of steels in molten

salt is the selective dissolution of Cr [6], the thickness of the Cr-depleted layer is a

major parameter for corrosion evaluation.  According to the Cr map in Fig. 6(c), the

degree of corrosion attack on 316L SS is slight after corrosion in molten FLiNaK salt

at 600 oC for 50 h.  In addition, a thin Fe-rich film was observed on the surface of the

316L SS after the corrosion experiment, as shown in Fig. 6(c).  Misra et al. [34]

demonstrated that the tendency for common alloying elements to be corroded in

fluoride salts increased in the following order: Ni < Co < Fe < Cr.  Thus, the existence

of FeF3 in the melt serves as an oxidant and can react with Cr and deposit on the surface

of the steel, resulting in the formation of Fe-rich layer and depletion of Cr in the near

surface area.

To further evaluate the effect of cold forging on the corrosion behavior of 316L SS,

the E-i behavior of 316L SS before and after cold forging was measured using

potentiodynamic polarization, and the results are shown in Fig. 8.  There are two

approaches to interpret Fig. 8, the first method is by understanding the shift in potential

regimes [35] and current density in relation to the thermodynamically stable phase in

the molten FLiNaK whereas the second is by comparing the electrochemical metrics

(e.g. corrosion current density) that provides a quantitative comparison of corrosion

behavior.  From Fig. 8, it is observed that cold forging shifts the E-i curve toward a

more positive potential (relative to Pt), suggesting an increase in nobility. Using the

Mixed Potential theory as an interpretation framework [36], corrosion potential (Ecorr)

describes a freely corroding, open-circuit condition in which the rate of anodic is

identical to that of cathodic reactions, and thus Ecorr is often described as open-circuit

oxidants concentration etc.) and kinetically determined (via mass-transport effects,

higher density of dislocations and grain boundaries in the material, more Cr reacts and

dissolve into the salt, resulting in a corrosion zone with more Ni and Fe compositions.

Since the half-cell redox potentials for Ni/NiF2 or Fe/FeF2 are higher than that of

of corrosion products that impose a mass-transport limitation which materials

microstructure is expected to have a limited effect [35,38].  The study of salt film

precipitation in molten FLiNaK is outside the scope of this manuscript and will be

further elaborated in our future work.

## 4. Discussion

By comparing Fig. 7 with Fig. 6, the Cr depletion depth of cold-forged 316L SS

is deeper than that of 316L SS after molten salt exposure, indicating that the cold work

accelerates corrosion of stainless steel in molten fluoride salts.  Based on

characterization of cold-forged 316L SS in Fig. 7, the main corrosion of the steel is by

the selective dissolution of Cr into the salt, resulting in the formation of some internal

voids within the material and a Cr depletion zone.

In molten fluoride salts, the Gibbs free energy of formation of various metal

fluorides indicate that the tendency for common alloy constituent to corrode increases

in the order: Mo, Ni, Co, Fe and Cr [6,34].  Thus, Cr of 316L SS is the primary

constituent that is most prone to corrosion.  In molten FLiNaK salt, the existence of

FeF3 reacts with Cr by the following reaction, resulting in the corrosion of Cr and

deposition of Fe film on the surface of the sample.

FeF3 + Cr = CrF3 + Fe (Δ ! = ˗152.3 kJ/mol at 600 oC) (3)

It is well known that the corrosion of stainless steel is the selective dissolution of Cr,

and the corrosion rate of steel in molten fluoride salt is controlled by the solid-state

diffusion of Cr from the steel matrix to the steel/salt interface [40].  As indicated, Cr

corrosion is much more thermodynamically prone to attack and spontaneous dissolution

according to standard Gibb’s free energy of reaction (3), which is calculated using HSC

chemistry 6.0 software.

However, transport processes may have considerably different rates depending on

details. Based on the solid-state diffusion mechanism, Cr diffuses through substitutional

diffusion when the presence of defects in 316L SS is sufficiently large and the activation

energy is sufficiently low [41].  The solid-state diffusion occurs not only along lattice

defects, but also takes place along line and surface defects, such as grain boundaries.

The diffusion is significantly influenced by the microstructure of the materials [41].

Wang et al. [42] reported that grain refinement greatly enhances the diffusion of Cr in

molten fluoride salt environments because of the contribution from boundary diffusion,

the effective diffusion rate of Cr in a fine-grained Ni-Cr alloy with grain size of 0.8 μm

is 7.5 times greater than that of 3 μm coarse-grained Ni-Cr alloy, indicating the grain

boundaries that are locations of atomic mismatch are open zones that facilitate diffusion.

Zheng et al. [43] revealed that the main corrosion of 316 SS is intergranular corrosion

and the Cr depletion predominantly occurred along the high angle grain boundaries

(HAGBs) and that the ∑3 grain boundaries were very resistant to corrosion in molten

fluoride salts.  Zhou et al. [44] reported that Cr more readily diffuses to HAGBs rather

than to low angle grain boundaries (LABGs), suggesting that the distribution and type

of grain boundaries significantly influence the diffusion behavior of Cr within the

material matrix. Consequently, it is concluded that cold forging alters the microstructure,

such as localized grain boundary strains, dislocation density etc., of alloys [45,46], and

therefore would change the corrosion resistance properties of materials.

According to the EBSD results in Fig. 3, cold forging has a significant impact on

the microstructure of 316L SS.  The KAM map in Fig. 4(c) shows a higher KAM value

throughout the grain of cold-forged 316L SS than that of as-received 316L SS (Fig.

4(a)), confirming that cold forging enhances the strain in the steel, especially near the

grain boundaries.  Compared with the local misorientation distributions in Fig. 4(b)

with Fig. 4(d), the kernel average misorientation of grains of the cold-forged 316L SS

reached 4.4o, which is much larger than that of as-received 316L SS (i.e. 0.8o),

indicating a considerable growth in the density of total dislocations in the materials

during the cold forging process.  As expected, the dislocation density calculated based

on the XRD results in Fig. 5 increased from 1.2×1015 m-2 to 3.3×1015 m-2 after cold

forge processing, indicating that the cold forging increases the dislocation density of

alloys.  It is known that the diffusion rate of Cr in solid state alloy relies on the defect

density and activation energy.  Cold forging could increase the defect concentrations

and therefore increases the possibility of substitutional diffusion of Cr.  Moreover, the

grain boundaries and dislocation diffusion generally have smaller activation energies

than lattice diffusion and as a result become preferred paths for Cr diffusion.  Therefore,

more Cr in the cold-forged 316L SS than that in the 316L SS can diffuse from the matrix

to the steel/salt interface and dissolved into the molten salt during the corrosion

experiment.  The consumption of Cr on the steel surface consequently accelerates the

diffusion of Cr from the matrix into surface due to the concentration gradient, especially


<!-- Page 19 -->


19

for the regions near the grain boundaries, leading to the serious grain boundaries

corrosion of cold forged 316L SS after exposure in molten FLiNaK salt at 600 oC for

50 h, as shown in Fig. 7.  Cold forging increases the density of high diffusion pathways

such as grain boundaries and dislocations, resulting in a higher Cr diffusion rate and

hence exacerbating the corrosion of the steel in molten fluoride salt.

## 5. Summary and Conclusions

In this work, the effect of cold forging on the microstructure and corrosion behavior

of 316L SS in high temperature molten salt was investigated. The microstructural

evolution and corrosion behavior of 316L SS before and after corrosion experiments in

molten FLiNaK salt were characterized and compared.   The main conclusions are as

follows:

(1) During the cold forging process, the 316L SS undergoes plastic deformation

under applied stress, leading to an increase in dislocation density within the

lattice, which promotes grain refinement and the formation of orientation.

(2) Based on the XRD, the dislocation density increased from 1.2×1015 m-2 to

3.3×1015 m-2 after cold forged to 50% reduction in thickness.

# The corrosion effects of neutron activation of 2LiF-BeF2 (FLiBe)

Lorenzo Vergari 1, Raluca O. Scarlat *,1, Ryan D. Hayes , Massimiliano Fratoni

Department of Nuclear Engineering, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA

A R T I C L E  I N F O

Keywords: Redox control in molten salts Tritium production Neutron-activation driven corrosion Irradiation-corrosion in molten salts FLiBe fusion blanket fluoride-salt cooled high-temperature reactor (FHR)

A B S T R A C T

The redox effect of activation reactions in molten salts has been previously qualitatively defined but never quantified. Here, we quantify the corrosion effects of neutron activation of FLiBe. Rates of change of activation products are computed for FHR and ARC. The impact of activation reactions on salt chemistry is quantitatively compared to other environmental effects of similar consequences on the salt. The results are applied to a redox control case-study and an irradiation-corrosion experiment. The results are presented in a manner useful to the reactor chemist and designer concerned with corrosion and chemistry control and tritium management in irradiated FLiBe, and design of salt-irradiation experiments.

## 1. Introduction

Fusion and fission nuclear reactors that employ 2LiF-BeF2 (FLiBe) as coolant or fuel solvent in the reactor core or in the blanket produce tritium primarily due to neutron activation of lithium and beryllium [1]. Tritium production, along with other activation reactions on FLiBe, is an oxidizing process that leads to corrosion of salt-facing metallic compo­ nents, in the absence of redox control [2–6]. Several types of nuclear reactors employ LiF-BeF2 mixtures. Fluoride-salt-cooled high-tempera­ ture reactors (FHRs) use molten FLiBe as coolant [7]. Thermal-spectrum molten salt reactors (MSRs) employ mixtures of LiF and BeF2 as the solvent for liquid fuel with high solubility for both actinides and fission products [8]. Tokamaks use FLiBe as the tritium breeding blanket and heat transfer medium [9]. Thus, it is of relevance to reactor designers and salt-irradiation experimentalists to have a methodology for quan­ tifying the chemical effects that arise from neutron activation reactions on FLiBe. Tritium production and all the other neutron activation reactions on Li, Be and F have chemical effects on the molten salt coolant by changing its redox potential and thus providing a continuous corrosion driver for metal components. In order to control degradation of metal components, chemistry control (i.e. redox control) must be employed to counteract the oxidizing (i.e. corrosive) effect of the neutron activation reactions [5]. The redox effect of activation reactions is acknowledged in litera­ ture reviews on molten salt corrosion [10-12] but it is not quantified. Furthermore, several computational studies on tritium production and

activation reactions across reactors are available in literature [13-22], but production rates of other hydrogen isotopes and oxygen isotopes in FLiBe have not yet been reported. Similarly, [23] identifies an interplay between tritium production and redox control, but does quantify the oxidizing effect of tritium production. The production rates and inventory build-up of all hydrogen isotopes and all other activation products [20,24] in FLiBe are analyzed here and the corresponding rates of corrosion product build-up are computed. The analyses in this paper are performed for an FHR advanced fission reactor and an Affordable, Robust, Compact (ARC)-class fusion blanket, using the University of California Berkeley (UCB) Mk-1 FHR [7] and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) ARC designs [25] as input parameters for these calculations. In addition to tritium production as an oxidizing process, Li breeding from Be and O breeding from F are also quantified as not-negligible contributions to the oxidizing effects of neutron irradiation in FLiBe. Furthermore, the production rate of the oxide anion is quantified, compared to other environmental effects that can lead to the introduction of oxide impurities in the fluoride melt, and discussed in the context of oxoacidity Pourbaix diagrams for FLiBe and their impact on corrosion. The results are applied to a redox control case-study and a prior irradiation-corrosion experiment. The impact on chemistry is quantified and quantitatively compared to other environmental effects with similar consequences on the salt chemistry. The effects of isotopic composition of lithium, operational time, reactor power, and primary salt inventory are then demonstrated. The results are normalized and generalized,

2.1. FLiBe activation reactions

Neutron irradiation of FLiBe produces tritium through neutron activation of its components (Table 1). The main pathway for tritium production is the (n, t) reaction on Li-6 (Equation 1 in Table 1). 2.2. The effects of activation reactions on redox state of the salt

In the molten salt, the redox potential of the salt can change as a consequence of neutron activation and nuclear decay. Table 2 lists the redox effects of each of the neutron activation reactions on FLiBe. For example, the neutron activation reaction 12 would lead to the chemical redox reaction 12 (Table 2). If the redox potential is controlled to a fixed value, then the relative amounts of each valence states can be computed from the law of mass action (i.e. from the chemical equilibrium constant). If the redox po­ tential is not controlled, then activation reactions will shift the redox potential, and hence will shift the relative concentration of the two valence states. In this case a coupled calculation can be performed that computes the final redox potential in the melt and the relative amounts of valence states of all the species present in the melt. For example, for the case of chromium oxidation by the oxidizing effect of tritium production the assumption of the predominant oxida­ tion state of tritium being 0 (H2) and not +1 (H+) needs to be verified for each specific concentration of Cr2+ in the salt, by considering the following chemical equilibrium reaction: 2H+ + Cr ↔equilibriumH2 + Cr2+. Assuming an upper bound of 750 appm Cr2+ in the salt and for simplicity a unitary activity of Cr metal and 1 atm total pressure, the ratio of partial pressures pH2/pHF = 5000 [5,36], so the tritium inventory in the gas phase that is in equilibrium with the salt is predominantly the oxidation state of zero (3H2). To determine the relative inventory in the

salt of the different valence states of tritium, the solubilities of 3HF and 3H2 in the salt must be known. At 600 ◦C the ratio of 3H2 to 3HF solu­ bilities in the salt is 0.0035 [6,35]3; thus the ratio of tritium concen­ trations in the salt is xH2/xHF = (5000)∗0.0035 = 18. Therefore, it is also reasonable to assume that tritium is predominantly in the oxidation state of zero for the dissolved tritium inventory in the salt. If the Cr2+ con­ centration is much above 750 appm (i.e., more oxidizing conditions), then a higher inventory of dissolved 3HF will be present in the salt and the assumption of tritium existin entirely in the oxidation state of 0 will begin to introduce errors in the calculation of oxidative effects from tritium production that are higher than 5%. In this case, the simplifying assumption of an oxidation state of zero for tritium would need to be replaced by a coupled calculation between redox potential drift and tritium inventory in its two valence states. However, a more oxidizing condition than the example considered here would be detrimental to metal corrosion, thus it is not expected to be of engineering relevance and the assumption of zero valence state for hydrogen isotopes is valid for most engineering applications.

4.1. Tritium production in the FHR and in ARC

The first row of Fig. 2 (results calculated from Equation 21 in Table 3) shows the tritium production rate (in mol 3H/day/ MWth) as a function of time, and its dependence on the isotopic composition of Li at the beginning of life of the coolant (BOL). For Li-6 enrichment (defined as mol Li-6 / (mol (Li-6 + Li-7)) on the order of tens to hundreds of appm (relevant to FHRs), the Mk-1 FHR BOL tritium production rate is on the order of 10-4 – 10-3 mol/day/MWth5. The tritium production rates cor­ responding to different BOL enrichment levels converge to the same equilibrium value to approximately 2.7 10-4 mol/day/MWth (assuming nominal salt inventory), after up to 50 years. The production rate at equilibrium is exclusively dependent on the ratio between the (n, α) cross section of Be-9 and the Li-6 absorption cross section [24]. The second row of Fig. 2 shows the Li-6 evolution with time. At equilibrium, the lithium enrichment converges to 13 appm. Because of

the functional form of Equation 21, given two reactors with different BOL Li enrichments, the difference in years required to reach the equi­ librium concentration is equal to the number of years that one of the two reactors would take to reach the BOL enrichment of the other one. The third row of Fig. 2 shows that the tritium production rate scales linearly with lithium enrichment; the linear function for Mk-1 FHR (μ mol H-3/ day/MWth = 62.5 + 5.45*(appm Li-6)) is valid for all other reactors with a similar neutron spectrum and hence similar averaged crosssections for Li-7, Li-6 and Be-9. The contribution of the different activation reactions to the tritium production rate is shown in Fig. 3. For Mk-1 FHR, considering a nominal 50 appm Li-6 at BOL, 81% of total tritium production is due to the activation of the Li-6 in fresh FLiBe and 19% comes from the (n, nα) reaction on Li-7 (Reaction 3). As irradiation proceeds, the initial in­ ventory of Li-6 is progressively consumed, and the tritium production is sustained by the Li-6 yielded by the (n, α) reaction on Be-9. At equilib­ rium, the two-step reaction on beryllium (Reactions 1, 2) is responsible for 53% of tritium production, the remainder being produced through Li-7 activation. It should be noted that the contribution from Li-7 ap­ pears to be constant with time because Li-7 depletion is negligible at the enrichment levels of interest for fission reactors (up to hundreds of appm of Li-6). At all times, tritium production from F-19 is negligible. For the ARC design at the nominal enrichment level of 90%, the main contrib­ utor to tritium production is Li-6, accounting for approximately 92% of the total production rate, followed by Li-7 (5%), F-19 (2%) and Be-9 (1%). Assuming that the blanket salt is constantly replenished to ensure a constant Li-6 inventory (see Fig. 10), tritium production rates are con­ stant with time. While tritium production rates in ARC are constant with time, they depend on the target isotopic composition of lithium in the salt and the tritium production rates does not increase monotonically with the Li-6 enrichment. This effect, which was previously shown in [39,43], is caused by the (n, nα) reaction on Li-7 (Equation 3), which occurs with fast neutrons in FLiBe. This reaction has a lower average cross section than the reaction on Li-6 (Equation 1), but also produces another neutron. As a result, a high Li-6 enrichment reduces the fre­ quency of the reaction on Li-7 and introduces a penalty on the neutron flux. For the ARC design, the tritium production rate is optimized at an enrichment level of approximately 25 at. % (consistent with the results in [39])6. This enrichment level is significantly lower than the 90% Li-6 enrichment proposed in the early design stage [25]. At 25 at. % Li-6, the contributors to H-3 production are Li-6 (60%), followed by Li-7 (37%), F-19 (2%) and Be-9 (1%).

In the Mk-1 FHR, if all produced tritium is assumed to be removed before it decays, tritium accounts for more than 98% of the total production rate of all hydrogen isotopes at BOL and 95% at equilibrium (Fig. 4a). If tritium and its daughter nuclide He-3 are never removed from the core, the (n,p) re­ action on He-3 causes a protium production rate larger than the tritium production rate, after 9 years of operation in FHR. The Mk-1 FHR will operate in the region between these two cases and its behavior could be approximated with the first case if the chemistry control system has the task of tritium removal. In ARC at the 90% Li-6 nominal enrichment level, tritium accounts for about 90% of the produced hydrogen (Fig. 4b). For ARC, we assume continuous tritium removal and Li-6 replenishment for the blanket, as discussed in Section 3.1; therefore, the scenario with in-core tritium decay is not considered for ARC.

4.5. Other FLiBe activation products

The main activation product for FLiBe besides tritium is oxygen (see Fig. 5). In Mk-1 FHR, the oxygen production rate is approximately 35% of the tritium production rate at BOL and 80% at equilibrium, and it is predominantly O-16. In ARC, the total oxygen production rate is 25% of the tritium production rate, with the 76% being O-16, the 19% being O- 18 and the remainder O-17. The oxygen production rate in the FHR could suggest that a fraction of the produced tritium will be in the form of tritiated water. Nevertheless, the produced oxygen might also remain as a dissolved anion O2–, produce a precipitated oxide (e.g Cr2O3), or (if the redox potential is extremely oxidizing) be oxidized to O2 gas, which in turn interacts with graphite or metals or is released into the cover gas. Carbon and nitrogen are also possible activation products in FLiBe. In the FHR, C and N production rates are negligible: carbon production rate is three orders of magnitude lower than oxygen production; nitrogen is more than ten orders of magnitude lower. In ARC, C-14 production about 2.4% of tritium production rate. This may suggest that a small fraction of the tritium may be present in the form of tritiated methane. The carbon produced in the salt could also speciate at carbonate anions in the salt, by complexing with O2–, may interact with or deposit on the graphite and metal surfaces, or may produce other carbon products that are soluble or suspended in the salt. Nitrogen production rates remain negligible in ARC.

5. Discussion: Chemical effects of the activation reactions in FLiBe.

5.1. The oxidizing effects of neutron activation reactions on FLiBe

The oxidizing effect of activation reactions in the salt has been qualitatively defined in [11,12,23] but never quantified. Here, we quantify the corrosion effect of the activation reactions in terms of rate of Cr oxidation or rate of sacrificial Be metal consumption. Fig. 6 shows the oxidizing effect contributions of each of the activation reactions on FLiBe.

5.1.1. FHR In an FHR at BOL, Cr would be consumed at rate of 13 mg Cr/day/ MWth and the main sources of oxidative effects are:

• the production of H-3 from Li-6 and Li-7, • the production of Li-6 from Be-9, and • the production of O-16 from F-19.

At steady state isotopic composition of lithium, each of these four reactions contribute at a similar rate to the oxidizing effect. Thus, at 13 ppm Li-6, the rate of tritium production accounts for only 50% of the total oxidative effects of activation reactions, at the nominal BOL 50 ppm Li-6 it accounts for 70%; at natural Li isotopic abundance the tritium produc­ tion would be the dominant oxidative activation reaction. The progression rate of the corrosion front that corresponds to a given rate of Cr oxidation depends on the heat exchanger surface area relative to the rate of the activation reactions. For a 236 MWth FHR with 224 m2 of heat exchanger surface area, the 13 mg Cr/day/MWth rate of Cr oxidation corresponds to a predicted corrosion front 7that moves at rate of 4 um/ year. This rate is comparable to the less than 1 um/year corrosion rate in a non-isothermal FLiBe loop that is at the lowest possible redox potential set by beryllium metal [56]. Thus, depending on the heat exchanger surface area relative to the rate of the activation reactions, it is likely that the corrosion due to the oxidizing effects of FLiBe activation is negligible relative to the rate of corrosion driven by the temperature

5.3. Case study: Redox control with addition of Be metal

For active redox control with Be metal, FHR BOL would require 0.54 g Be/day (0.20 kg Be/yr) for the 236 MWth Mk-1 FHR. Assuming a solubility of Be metal in FLiBe of 0.3 mol% (with MWFLiBe = 33 g/mol) [66,67] and the Mk-1 FHR primary salt inventory of 92 ton, there can be an inventory of 75 kg of dissolved Be metal, which is sufficiently abundant to neutralize the effects of activation reactions on FLiBe for the entire reactor lifetime. Otherwise stated, the Be that is needed for redox

control of activation reactions has a 400-year residence time if Be metal is at its solubility limit in BOL FLiBe and is consumed at the rate dictated by the oxidation effect of activation reactions. ARC would require 10 gBe/day (3.68 kg Be/yr) (Fig. 6). Assuming a solubility of Be metal in FLiBe of 0.3 mol% [66] and the ARC salt in­ ventory of 960 ton, there can be an inventory up to 790 kg of dissolved Be metal in the FLiBe inventory. Otherwise stated, the Be that is needed for redox control of activation reactions has a 200-year residence time if Be metal is at its solubility limit in BOL FLiBe and is consumed at the rate dictated by the oxidation effect of activation reactions. Given the uncertainty in the solubility of Be metal in FLiBe, it might be the case that continuous addition of a redox control agent or sacri­ ficial metal is necessary for the ARC blanket, which has a high volu­ metric tritium generation rate (7 mmol H-3/day/m3 of salt inventory). LiF may need to be replenished at rate proportional to the Be redox agent consumption, to avoid changing the composition of the FLiBe towards higher BeF2 molar ratios, which eventually will have a higher salt vis­ cosity and higher vapor pressure [68,69]. 4 kg Be/yr would require replenishing LiF at a rate of 22 kg LiF/yr. LiF replenishing is also needed for the second reason of replenishing the Li-6 isotope that is being consumed by tritium production reactions. Without LiF replenishing, Be metal addition would lead to a change in FLiBe composition of 0.02 mol % BeF2 per year, so LiF replenishing to balance Be additions is negligible at these Be addition rates. Conversely, if Li-6 resupply is needed, depending on the enrichment in the LiF feed, BeF2 additions may be needed to balance LiF additions.

The impact of FLiBe activation reactions on the chemistry of the molten salt is quantified and compared to other environmental effects with similar consequences on the salt chemistry. The results, summarized in Table 11, are presented in a manner useful to the reactor chemist and the reactor designer concerned with corrosion control and chemistry control and tritium management for irradiated FLiBe salt in fission and fusion reactors and for salt-irradiation experiments. Redox control should consider both the direct effect of oxidation from activation reactions, and the indirect effect of a redox

potential shift on the rate of corrosion driven by temperature gradients in a flow loop. Design of salt-irradiation experiments investigating metal corrosion (Section 5.4) should account for: (1) lithium isotopic compo­ sition of the salt (and its depletion, if relevant for the duration of irra­ diation) (Fig. 2 and Fig. 3), (2a) all of the activation reactions with redox contributions (Table 2, Fig. 6 ), (2b) all other inventories or sources of oxidants, and (3) the total surface area of the salt-facing metal. For corrosion prediction in an FHR or ARC reactor, or in a flowing loop with neutron irradiation, the additional consideration of total salt inventory may be needed. This study did not include the activation of dilute species inadver­ tently present in the salt, such as uranium or potassium or transition metals. The impact of impurities on the neutronic performance of FLiBe has been previously studied by [57], but the chemical and corrosion effects of the activation reactions of solutes in the salt remain topics of future study.
