# Rapid directed evolution guided by protein language models and epistatic interactions

**Authors:** Vincent Q. Tran; Matthew Nemeth; Liam J. Bartie; Sita S. Chandrasekaran; Alison Fanton; Hyungseok C. Moon; Brian L. Hie; Silvana Konermann; Patrick D. Hsu

**Affiliations:** 1Arc Institute, 3181 Porter Drive, Palo Alto, CA, USA | 2Department of Chemistry, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA | 3Department of Bioengineering, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA | 4University of California, Berkeley - University of California, San Francisco Graduate Program in Bioengineering, Berkeley, CA, USA | 5Department of Chemical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA | 6Stanford Data Science, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA | 7Department of Biochemistry, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, CA, USA | 8Center for Computational Biology, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA

## Abstract

Protein engineering is limited by the inefficient search through a high-dimensional sequence space to find combinations of synergistic mutations. Traditional approaches use stepwise mutation stacking, while machine learning methods require extensive datasets or multiple experimental rounds and are bottlenecked by costly, length-limited gene synthesis. We present MULTI-evolve, a rapid evolution framework that systematically engineers multi-mutants. Our approach combines protein language models or existing functional data with epistatic modelling to predict synergistic combinations. Proposed multi-mutants are built through MULTI-assembly, a mutagenesis method enabling high-efficiency assembly across multi-kilobase sequences. Applying MULTI-evolve to three proteins achieved up to 10-fold improvements with a single round of machine learning-guided directed evolution. MULTI-evolve provides a streamlined approach for end-to-end, multi-mutant engineering for a broad range of protein types and functions.

Proteins power diverse functions across all forms of life, and through directed evolution and engineering, these functions have enabled applications from industrial enzymes to human therapeutics. The function of a protein is directly encoded in its sequence of amino acids. However, a protein of length N has 20N possible variants, where only a minuscule fraction are functional (1). Natural evolution has used billions of years of random exploration to identify these functional needles in a haystack. For modern biotechnology and therapeutic applications, we need to solve this astronomical search problem in months or years, which has motivated the development of accelerated engineering methods.

Directed evolution (DE) methods have improved protein engineering by mimicking slow evolutionary processes in an accelerated manner (1–5). Recently, DE methods have also been enhanced using machine learning (6, 7). By leveraging models to perform in silico variant screening, machine learning-guided directed evolution (MLDE) covers broader search spaces and mitigates experimental screening (8, 9). However, the predictive power of these models depends on learning epistatic effects in the target protein, where the functional impact of one amino acid mutation can alter others (10). The inability to learn these epistatic effects leads to poor prediction of enhanced variants, particularly when training datasets display a low proportion of function-enhancing mutations (11, 12). MLDE methods improve the ability to predict and discover enhanced variants by depending on rational mechanistic insights to target key residues or laborious experimental work with multiple engineering rounds and extensive variant screening (11–17). Compounding these limitations, computationally nominated variants are difficult to physically generate with conventional methods for experimental evaluation, especially for large proteins. Existing cloning methods display low assembly efficiencies, involve subjective mutagenic oligo design, or require tedious workflows (18–20). MLDE methods resort to commercial DNA synthesis that bottlenecks experimentation due to costs and turnaround times, which scale with protein length and the number of tested variants (14, 21). Collectively, these limitations result in non-generalizable methods, where implementation is inefficient and often relies on protein-specific mechanistic knowledge.

To overcome the current challenges with MLDE, we present MULTI-evolve, a machine learning-guided end-to-end framework capable of rapidly engineering any protein of interest. MULTI-evolve (model-guided, universal, targeted installation of multi-mutants) evolves proteins through the design and synthesis of hyperactive multi-mutants by combining the strengths of protein language models (PLMs), epistasis-aware modeling, and multi-site mutagenesis. We applied MULTI-evolve to engineer three complex and distinct proteins: engineered soybean ascorbate peroxidase (APEX), known for its intricate redox mechanism, CRISPR-Cas13d, which engages in complex RNA-guided interactions, and an anti-CD122 antibody, which requires optimization of multiple translationally relevant properties (22–25). Across the three proteins, our framework initially identified single mutants with up to 3-fold improvement, using PLMs or existing functional data, and efficiently learned key epistatic interactions to engineer hyperactive multi-mutants, containing up to seven mutations and displaying up to 256-fold improvement. We designed these multi-mutants with a single MLDE round, outperforming methods that demand multiple rounds or extensive screening. Additionally, MULTI-evolve provides an end-to-end framework using MULTI-assembly, our multi-site mutagenesis method that constructs multi-mutants with 40-70% efficiency across multiple kilobases of protein coding sequence and reduces turnaround times from weeks to days. Together, MULTI-evolve establishes a new paradigm for protein engineering where complex multi-mutants can be rapidly designed and synthesized for any protein target.

## Results

### Development and benchmarking of the MULTI-evolve framework

Protein engineering requires navigating vast sequence spaces to find synergistic mutations that enhance function. Traditional DE methods rely on minimally exploratory stepwise walks, which evaluate one new mutation at a time (Fig. 1A). More recent MLDE approaches perform in silico variant screening to search more broadly; however, accurate model-guided extrapolation to enhanced multi-mutants depends on multiple iterative rounds of extensive experimental validation (Fig. 1B). To overcome these limitations, we developed MULTI-evolve (model-guided, universal, targeted installation of multi-mutants), a framework designed to “jump” directly to hyperactive multi-mutants in a single MLDE round (Fig. 1C). The complete framework integrates three key components: PLM-based mutation discovery, machine learning for epistasis modeling, and efficient multi-site mutagenesis. Here, we describe the systematic development and validation of each component that enables this integrated approach.

While single mutations can improve protein function, substantial enhancements often require multiple beneficial mutations acting in concert. Recent work has validated the ability of PLM-based zero-shot predictors to efficiently identify function-enhancing mutations through an understanding of evolutionary fitness (26). Each PLM learns distinct evolutionary patterns from biological data that guide predictions toward mutations of high evolutionary fitness, which can translate to improved functional activity (27, 28) (Fig. 2A). However, individual methods often identify few function-enhancing mutations and may fail entirely for certain proteins when their learned evolutionary biases do not align with the function of interest (29). We hypothesized that combining multiple PLM zero-shot methods would discover more beneficial mutations available for combination (Fig. 2A). In addition, we reasoned that an ensemble of methods could mitigate method-specific biases that lead to protein-specific failures. Through comprehensive benchmarking across 73 diverse deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets, we developed a PLM zero-shot ensemble to comprehensively identify function-enhancing mutations (Fig. 2B, S1A,B, see Supplementary Text). PLM zero-shot methods employ the widely-used fold-change likelihood score, which calculates the log-likelihood ratio of a mutation relative to wild-type. We observed PLMs exhibit biases against specific residues such as proline and bulky aromatics, assigning low fold-change scores to these mutations (Fig. S1C,D). To normalize for these biases and enable fair discovery of all residues, we utilize a z-scoring strategy that normalizes fold-change scores by amino acid mutation type, and we find that this strategy leads to comparable hit rates (Fig. S1E–F). We integrate these complementary scoring strategies into a PLM ensemble approach that utilizes structure-informed (e.g. ESM-IF) and non-structure-informed PLMs (e.g. ESM1v, ESM2). By combining four distinct PLM methods, our ensemble approach identifies more than 20 function-enhancing mutations compared to standalone PLM methods that only identify up to 11 function-enhancing mutations each (Fig. 2C).

Having established the capability for single mutant discovery, the next critical component was developing a model for MULTI-evolve to predict multi-mutant fitness. Proteins often exhibit complex epistasis where mutational effects can combine non-linearly to create rugged fitness landscapes (10). While fully connected neural networks (FCNNs) can learn epistatic interactions to extrapolate to multi-mutants (11, 30), how the training dataset composition affects extrapolation across diverse protein datasets has not been thoroughly characterized. We hypothesized that double mutants capture sufficient epistatic information for accurate extrapolation to higher order mutants, while remaining experimentally feasible. To test this hypothesis and identify the extrapolation limits of the models, we benchmarked FCNN performance across published deep mutational scanning datasets spanning diverse protein families (12, 31–33) (Fig. 2D). Models trained on different compositions of variants were systematically evaluated for their ability to predict held-out multi-mutant fitness. Across all proteins tested, incorporating double mutants in the training set markedly improved predictive performance over single mutants alone, with triple mutants providing additional boost (Fig. 2E). In addition, models trained on double mutants extrapolated well to combinations of 8-12 mutations (Fig. 2F, Fig. S3A). Together, our benchmarking results exhibit that double mutants enable data-efficient training with strong extrapolation to multi-mutants across diverse protein families.

We next validated the MULTI-evolve models against existing methods to predict multi-mutant fitness (Fig. 2G). We compared the MULTI-evolve models to alignment-based models, PLM-based zero-shot predictors, inverse folding models, and few shot learning approaches including ESM MSA Transformer and EVOLVEpro (13, 26, 29, 34–40) (Fig. 2G). Our MULTI-evolve models outperformed all tested methods in both predictive accuracy and precision for identifying high-fitness multi-mutants containing 3-10 mutations (Fig. 2H–I). We quantified the model precision as the recovery of multi-mutants in the top fifth percentile. MULTI-evolve models exceeded 50% precision in 7 of 12 proteins, versus 4 for the next best approach, and were able to recover high-fitness multi-mutants across all proteins (Fig. 2I). To further validate the ability of MULTI-evolve for data-efficient learning, we tested whether MULTI-evolve maintains accuracy in lower data regimes (low-N). To perform low-N benchmarking (Fig. S3D), we randomly sampled single mutants and their combinatorial variants in each protein dataset. Models trained on these subsets, which constituted less than 300 variants or 10% of the available singles and doubles, still accurately predicted multi-mutant activity compared to training on the full set of singles and doubles (Pearson’s R, 0.64 versus 0.56, respectively) (Fig. S3E). As in the larger data regimes, the MULTI-evolve models surpassed baseline protein prediction methods (Fig. S3F). Together, our benchmarking results validate data-efficient learning through double mutant characterization, eliminating the need to experimentally test thousands of variants for training data.

With the ability to reliably propose candidate multi-mutant variants, we established the final component of our method, MULTI-assembly (Fig. 2J), to enable rapid variant synthesis for experimental validation. Building on previously established multi-site mutagenesis methods, MULTI-assembly was systematically optimized by refining reaction conditions to achieve high build efficiencies (40-70%) and streamline reaction conditions, which reduced protocol time for gene construction by 50% (18, 19, 41, 42) (see Supplementary Text for more details). Additionally, we ensured the reliability of MULTI-assembly by developing a computational oligo designer (see Data, code, and materials availability), which we used to design all oligos for cloning multi-mutants in this study.

In practice, MULTI-evolve operates as follows (Fig. 2K): starting from any protein of interest, we first identify function-enhancing single mutants using either our PLM zero-shot ensemble or existing functional data such as deep mutational scanning. We then experimentally characterize all pairwise combinations of the top ~15 mutations (n ≤ C(15,2)), generating a compact but information-rich dataset that captures key epistatic interactions. This data trains the MULTI-evolve model that learns the epistatic landscape and extrapolates to predict activities for all possible higher-order combinations. To nominate multi-mutants, our experimental testing observed enhancements in function for variants up to seven mutations. Given this observation, we recommend selecting multi-mutants containing up to seven mutations, ranking them by predicted activity, and rapidly synthesizing the top candidates via MULTI-assembly for experimental validation. While prior studies have individually explored PLMs, epistasis modeling, or multi-site mutagenesis, our systematic integration of these methods into a single end-to-end workflow enables practical engineering of hyperactive multi-mutants in a single MLDE round, reducing the iterative cycles and extensive screening that often bottleneck protein engineering campaigns. Our PLM zero-shot ensemble approach enables discovery of many function-enhancing mutations to rapidly initialize evolution to hyperactive multi-mutants, which is supported by our optimized implementations of epistatic learning and multi-site mutagenesis. With this framework established, we sought to demonstrate MULTI-evolve across three diverse protein targets: APEX, CRISPR-Cas13d, and an anti-CD122 antibody.

### Engineering hyperactive APEX multi-mutants with MULTI-evolve

The evolutionary trajectory of a protein can be biased by its initial mutations, getting trapped in local maxima (9). We hypothesized that MULTI-evolve’s focus on learning of epistatic landscapes for extrapolation would make it robust to different initialization strategies, whether mutations come from PLM predictions, experimental screens, or prior engineering efforts. As a proof of concept, we used MULTI-evolve to evolve the engineered soybean ascorbate peroxidase (APEX). APEX displays a fast, high dynamic range readout, and known variants exist for comparison, specifically APEX2 (which we also refer to as the A134P mutant) (22, 43). To initialize MULTI-evolve for APEX engineering, we employed our PLM zero-shot ensemble approach to identify function-enhancing single mutants. To readout APEX activity, we used a fluorescence-based assay with the Amplex Red substrate, where APEX-mediated oxidation produces the red fluorescent molecule, resorufin (Fig. 3A).

Using our PLM zero-shot ensemble approach, we nominated and experimentally evaluated a set of 82 mutations across 62 positions. With the ensemble approach, we identified 16 function-enhancing mutations across APEX (Fig. 3B). Only our z-scoring strategy successfully identified the hyper-enhancing A134P mutation, which was systematically penalized by standard fold-change scoring due to evolutionary biases against proline substitutions. This discovery exemplifies the utility of our ensemble scoring approach. By integrating methods with complementary evolutionary biases, the ensemble captures beneficial mutations that would be missed by any single approach and increases the total number of hits, defined as a mutation that enhances activity greater than 1.4-fold over wild-type (Fig. 3C). Beyond the A134P mutant, we collectively identified 15 novel mutations that enhanced APEX activity by 1.4 to 2.7-fold, with mutations discovered through one or multiple PLM methods (Fig. 3D). The surface localization of most mutations suggests their effects may be mediated through improved protein stabilization (Fig. 3E). Besides A134P, the only active-site proximal mutation is I185V. I185 coordinates the sodium ion in the active site, and we infer the valine substitution may reduce local hydrophobicity to improve coordination (Fig. 3F,G). Overall, our results with APEX validate the ability of our PLM zero-shot ensemble approach to identify function-enhancing mutations, such as the hyper-enhancing A134P mutation, providing a rich mutational set for MULTI-evolve to build higher order combinations.

With our set of function-enhancing mutations, we challenged MULTI-evolve to improve the A134P mutant. The A134P mutant already exhibits substantially enhanced activity over wild-type APEX, making further activity improvements difficult. Nevertheless, we applied MULTI-evolve to combine the A134P variant with these newly identified mutations. We generated and measured the activities of all pairwise combinations of the selected function-enhancing mutations, with the majority of double mutants displaying synergistic or subadditive epistatic interactions (Fig. S6A). With the resultant single and double-mutant dataset, we trained the MULTI-evolve model to model the epistatic landscape. For model training, we performed a hyperparameter grid search to find the optimal sequence encodings and model architecture. Comparing one-hot encodings, physicochemical descriptors (AAindex, Georgiev), and protein language model embeddings (ESM2-3B, ESMC-6B) (40, 44–46), we found encoding sequences with one-hot encodings to consistently perform the best across all model architectures. Additionally, model performance decreased with an increasing number of hidden layers (Fig. S7A). Using the optimized model architecture, we predicted the activity of all possible 5- to 7-mutation variants and selected the top three variants per mutational load. The resulting variants showed remarkable improvements, with fold improvement values ranging from 193- to 256-fold over APEX and 3.6- to 4.8-fold over the A134P mutant (Fig. 3H). Notably, each multi-mutant achieved higher activities than their respective constituent double mutant combinations, from 5.5- to 8.7-fold, indicating that MULTI-evolve successfully proposed multi-mutants with improved synergy (Fig. S6B).

Through engineering the A134P mutant, APEX2, we considered whether our engineering was exploiting a narrow fitness peak contingent on the presence of the hyperactivating A134P mutation. Therefore, we asked whether MULTI-evolve could be used to produce synergistic multi-mutants leveraging epistatic effects across sites without the highly function-enhancing A134P mutation. As before, our set of double mutants displayed various types of epistatic interactions from synergistic to antagonistic (Fig. S6C) Using the same train and test setup to model these epistatic interactions, we selected and evaluated the top three variants per mutational load. Although still approximately 2-fold less active than the A134P mutant, our MULTI-evolve variants exhibited fold improvement values ranging from 11 to 13.5-fold relative to wild-type APEX (Fig. 3I). Notably, MULTI-evolve outperformed a recent MLDE framework, EVOLVEpro, which only improved activity up to 1.9-fold improvement after five rounds (13) (Fig. 3I). The best mutant from EVOLVEpro was G50R, which was a mutation we nominated with our PLM zero-shot ensemble approach. To further evaluate the extrapolation capabilities of our MULTI-evolve model, we tested even higher-order variants containing eight and nine mutations, and although higher in activity than wild-type APEX (4.8- to 6.0-fold), we did not observe additional improvements in activity above the best double mutants (Fig. S6E). Similar to the A134P mutant engineering, each of our multi-mutants exceeded the activities of their constituent double mutants from 2.2- to 3.1-fold, demonstrating MULTI-evolve learned synergistic interactions (Fig. S6D). In addition, our 7-mutation variants (v802, v803, v804) achieved high assembly efficiencies of 50.9%, 69.8%, and 66.4%, respectively, with MULTI-assembly (Fig. S6F–H). Together, our APEX and APEX2 mutant engineering establishes the ability of MULTI-evolve to efficiently learn the epistatic landscape from a compact dataset of double mutants and extrapolate to synergistic combinations.

Next, we sought to mechanistically characterize our top APEX variants from both engineering campaigns. Our best variant without A134P, v804, achieved 20-fold improvement over APEX in biotin labelling activity, reaching 80% of the A134P mutant’s labelling efficiency (Fig. 3J,K). Our top A134P mutation-containing variants, v831 and v834, achieved 1.3-fold improvement in biotin labelling activity compared to the A134P mutant (Fig. 3K). Importantly, all variants maintained expression levels comparable to APEX and the A134P mutant, confirming that activity improvements were not due to altered protein expression (Fig. 3L). Compared to APEX, v804 also displayed improved Amplex Red-oxidation (Fig. S6J, K) and enzyme kinetics measured through a guaiacol steady-state assay, exhibiting a 1.5-fold improvement in kcat/km (Fig. S6I, Fig. 3M–O). For our A134P-containing variants, v806, v831, and v834 also displayed enhanced Amplex Red-oxidation (Fig. S6L) and enzyme kinetics compared to the A134P mutant, exhibiting 1.2- to 1.5-fold improvement in kcat/km (Fig. S6I, Fig. 3N, O). These results confirm that MULTI-evolve, using PLM-nominated mutations, identified functionally relevant epistatic interactions that directly enhance biochemical catalysis rather than through improving cellular expression.

### Engineering hyperactive dCasRx multi-mutants with MULTI-evolve

To demonstrate the generalizability of this approach, we next chose to engineer a CRISPR-Cas protein system for trans-splicing applications with MULTI-evolve (Fig. 4A). RNA-targeting Cas proteins have been leveraged for two major RNA splicing applications: 1) manipulation of alternative cis-splicing by exon exclusion or exon activation (23, 47, 48) and 2) programmable incorporation of recombinant exon(s) into a target pre-mRNA transcript, or trans-splicing (49, 50). Among the RNA-targeting Cas proteins, the CRISPR-Cas13d ortholog, CasRx, has been shown to be the one of the most effective orthologs in human cells (23, 51). However, splicing modulation by the catalytically inactive form, dCasRx, often requires either fusion to splicing factors or pairing with additional protein modules, which complicates delivery for therapeutic applications (47, 50). We therefore aimed to improve dCasRx’s intrinsic functionality to modulate the splicing of endogenous human transcripts.

Having successfully engineered APEX using PLM-nominated mutations, for dCasRx we explored whether MULTI-evolve could achieve similar results when initialized using experimental functional data. Protein engineers often have access to mutations identified through prior directed evolution campaigns, deep mutational scans, or structure-guided studies that could be leveraged by MULTI-evolve. To test this scenario, we generated a functional dataset for dCasRx via DMS to comprehensively analyze all possible single amino acid dCasRx variants for their effects on exon exclusion activity (Fig. 4B–D, Fig. S8–13). Using the functional data from our DMS assay, we nominated single mutations for their ability to enhance CRISPR-guided trans-splicing using an assay where dCasRx is paired with a guided trans-splicing module (gTSM) or, in the context of the RNA-guided trans-splicing with Cas editor (RESPLICE) tool, both a gTSM and a Cas7-11-based cis interfering module (CIM) (50) (Fig. 4E–F, Fig. S14). Several mutations showed improvements, ranging from 1.3- to 2.8-fold over wild-type (Fig. 4G). Structural analysis revealed that enhancing mutations clustered in functional regions. Multiple mutations at E282 and S354P occur proximal to the crRNA:target RNA duplex, suggesting enhanced target RNA binding (Fig. 4H). The P91K mutation occurs near the crRNA direct repeat loop and likely improves crRNA recognition through a mutation to the more positively charged lysine group (Fig. 4H).

Having successfully identified function-enhancing mutations, we used MULTI-evolve to engineer hyperactive multi-mutants. We chose the top 15 single mutations, and evaluated a set of double mutants, observing prevalent epistatic interactions between mutations (Fig. S15A). Based on this dataset, we trained the MULTI-evolve model by performing a hyperparameter grid search. Similar to APEX, our grid search revealed that encoding sequences with one-hot encodings consistently performed best across model architectures and that model performance decreased as the number of hidden layers increased (Fig. S7B). For APEX, we observed diminishing gains in activity when surpassing seven mutations; therefore, moving forward, we chose to only test variants up to seven mutations (Fig. S6E). Using the optimized model architecture, we chose to predict activities for all possible 5- to 7-mutation variants and selected the top three variants per mutational load.

The MULTI-evolve variants showed substantial improvements, with activities ranging from 2.8- to 9.8-fold over wild-type dCasRx (Fig. 4I). The majority of the multi-mutants often surpassed the activities of their component double mutants by up to 3.5-fold, again displaying MULTI-evolve’s ability to identify synergistic interactions (Fig. S15B). In addition, the 7-mutation variants (v530, v531, v532) achieved sufficient MULTI-assembly efficiencies of 44.9%, 47.9%, and 46.4%, respectively (Fig. S15C–E). To further evaluate our dCasRx multi-mutants, we evaluated their trans-splicing efficiency across three endogenous genes: ITGB1, TFRC, and SMARCA4. When paired with the gTSM targeting the endogenous transcripts of the target gene, our variants consistently exhibited enhanced trans-splicing activity compared to wild-type dCasRx, achieving average improvements of 3.9- to 4.5-fold across all genes (Fig. 4J–L). In the context of RESPLICE, involving both a gTSM and a CIM, the variants maintained consistent enhancement of trans-splicing efficiency across all genes, showing an average 1.3-fold improvement (Fig. 4M–O). Similar to APEX, MULTI-evolve efficiently modelled the epistatic landscape of dCasRx to discover highly enhanced variants. Additionally, our dCasRx engineering demonstrates that MULTI-evolve can leverage diverse mutation sources for engineering, from computational PLM predictions to experimental screens, providing flexibility for protein engineers regardless of their available starting data.

### Multi-objective antibody design with MULTI-evolve

Multi-objective optimization is a common challenge in protein design, where molecular engineers seek to enhance multiple functional properties simultaneously rather than through iterative, single-parameter campaigns. This is particularly evident in antibody therapeutics, where translational utility depends on achieving optimal binding and expression in addition to other parameters such as immunogenicity or solubility (25). To demonstrate MULTI-evolve’s applicability for multi-objective optimization, we selected HuABC2, an antibody targeting CD122 (the shared β-chain of IL-2 and IL-15 receptors) relevant to autoimmune conditions including vitiligo, celiac disease, and eosinophilic esophagitis (24, 52–54) (Fig. 5A). HuABC2 exhibits potent binding (EC50 = 2.7 nM), providing an ideal test case where MULTI-evolve could improve binding and expression, a known developability parameter. This multi-objective task challenges MULTI-evolve to navigate trade-offs between mutations that improve expression versus those that affect residues critically involved in binding.

Having validated that PLM zero-shot methods can identify function-enhancing mutations with APEX, we asked whether these approaches could optimize two properties at once. We applied our PLM zero-shot ensemble to identify mutations that could enhance HuABC2 expression and its binding affinity to CD122. The ensemble nominated 132 mutations across both variable domains for experimental characterization. To enable rapid evaluation of expression and binding, we developed a high-throughput assay that utilizes HiBiT-tagged antibodies and a previous high-throughput ELISA-based assay to measure binding (Fig. 5B) (55). In our assay, expression of antibodies is measured and compared with a wild-type control to produce a relative expression score. Thereafter, we measure binding with ELISA and use relative expression scores to normalize and produce a relative binding score. We validated that the HiBiT tag does not affect affinity of the wild-type antibody and that it could be used as a proxy of the amount of antibody in a crude supernatant (Fig. S16). Single mutant screening revealed a diverse range of expression phenotypes, with several variants demonstrating substantial improvements over wild-type (Fig. 5C). Using our criterion of 1.2-fold improvement as the threshold for function-enhancing mutations, we identified multiple hits with the collective ensemble of PLM methods (Fig. 5D). The PLM ensemble approach successfully identified 19 mutations that enhanced expression by 1.1- to 2.0-fold, while affecting binding by 0.9- to 1.4-fold (Fig. 5F). Structural mapping of these mutations onto the AlphaFold3-predicted HuABC2-CD122 complex revealed that while most mutations occurred in framework regions, a few mutations occurred in complementarity-determining regions (Fig. 5E). These results establish that our PLM zero-shot ensemble approach can successfully balance competing objectives in antibody engineering, identifying mutations that enhance manufacturability without sacrificing therapeutic function.

The multi-objective optimization of HuABC2 presented a particularly challenging test case for MULTI-evolve, as our efforts must navigate complex trade-offs between competing functional properties. Unlike single-parameter optimization where mutations can be ranked linearly, multi-objective landscapes create Pareto frontiers where improvements in one property may compromise another. Our observation that double mutants displayed diverse epistatic interactions, including subadditive for expression and substantial antagonistic effects for binding (Fig. S17A,B), exemplifies the complex mutational dependencies that make multi-objective optimization a challenging process.

Training models on this epistatic landscape, we predicted activities for multi-mutants containing 3-7 mutations, selecting the top six variants per mutational load based on their position along the expression-binding Pareto frontier. Using our high-throughput assay, we observed the resulting multi-mutants to achieve up to 2.0- to 5.0-fold combined enhancement in relative binding and expression (Fig. 5G), with expression improvements of 2.0- to 4.0-fold and binding enhancements up to 1.5-fold (Fig. 5H). Critically, multiple multi-mutants surpassed the performance of their constituent double mutants up to 2.5-fold (Fig. S17C), demonstrating that MULTI-evolve successfully learned the distinct epistatic patterns governing each property and identified higher-order combinations that navigate around antagonistic interactions while amplifying beneficial ones. To further validate our engineered variants, we next expressed our variants at a larger scale and purified them (Fig. 5I, Fig. S17D). We quantified antibody expression yield via a specific anti-IgG ELISA assay and found the multi-mutants demonstrated 1.8- up to 6.5-fold improvements in expression yield (Fig. 5J, Fig. S17E). We further quantified the affinity of our top variants, observing 2.1- to 2.7-fold improvements in EC50 (Fig. 5K, L, Fig. S17E). Although our high-throughput assay enabled rapid initial characterization, our secondary validation experiments demonstrated that MULTI-evolve enabled robust improvements in both expression and affinity (Fig. S17F,G).

These results highlight MULTI-evolve’s key strength: its ability to learn function-enhancing mutations and property-specific epistatic architectures in order to predict multi-mutants that optimize across competing objectives. We demonstrate that MULTI-evolve can further improve the binding affinity of low nM binders, from 2.7 nM to 1.0 nM, while simultaneously improving expression yield. Critically, MULTI-evolve’s modular framework readily extends to any measurable protein property. By incorporating assays for additional parameters such as serum half-life, immunogenicity, or solubility, the same epistatic learning approach can simultaneously optimize across additional dimensions. The framework’s data-efficient training (requiring only ~100-200 double mutants) makes it practical to characterize variants across several readouts in parallel, enabling comprehensive multi-parameter optimization from a single experimental campaign. Here, we simultaneously improve both expression and binding affinity for an anti-CD122 antibody, displaying the capability of MULTI-evolve for therapeutic protein development where success requires balancing manufacturability, efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetic properties.

## Discussion

Here, we present MULTI-evolve, a machine learning-guided framework that overcomes the challenge of a massive search space for protein engineering by bridging evolutionary PLM priors with epistatic modelling to access synergistic higher-order combinations. Across three diverse proteins–APEX, Cas13d, and an anti-CD122 antibody–our framework engineered variants with 2- to 256-fold improvement, demonstrating broad applicability and multi-objective optimization capabilities. Its ability to predict the activity of multi-mutants is robust regardless of whether initial mutations are identified computationally through PLMs or experimentally through functional screens. With MULTI-assembly, we enable an end-to-end platform that achieves 40-70% synthesis efficiency for complex multi-mutants, avoids subjective mutagenic oligo design, and eliminates commercial DNA synthesis bottlenecks. Lastly, we developed a MULTI-evolve Design Tool to train models, predict multi-mutants, and design MULTI-assembly oligos for cloning (see Data, code, and materials availability). Together, our work establishes a user-friendly framework to rapidly design complex multi-mutants for any protein target.

Many MLDE approaches exhibit challenging trade-offs between experimental burden and predictive performance, requiring either extensive datasets, multiple MLDE rounds, deep mechanistic knowledge for targeted mutagenesis, or reliance on commercial gene synthesis (11–17). MULTI-evolve overcomes these limitations through three key innovations: (1) data-efficient learning (~100-200 variants), (2) single MLDE round extrapolation, and (3) optimized, rapid multi-site mutagenesis. In developing MULTI-evolve, we benchmarked PLM zero-shot methods and supervised FCNNs to enable data-efficient extrapolation to multi-mutants. We show that a PLM ensemble approach improves discovery of high-fitness single mutations compared to conventional implementation of PLM zero-shot predictors, identifying as many as 20 function-enhancing mutations. Our MULTI-evolve models outperform existing baseline methods in both predictive performance and precision for protein property prediction (Fig. 2D–I, S3). In our experimental work, we compare APEX engineering with MULTI-evolve to EVOLVEpro. This recently reported MLDE framework, which uses PLM embeddings combined with regression modeling to guide directed evolution, requires extensive iterative rounds of single mutant prediction and testing, followed by a final round that combines the function-enhancing mutations into multi-mutants. After five engineering rounds with EVOLVEpro for APEX engineering, we only improved activity up to 1.9-fold with the G50R mutation, which is a mutation nominated by our PLM zero-shot ensemble approach. In contrast, MULTI-evolve generated APEX variants with up to 13.5-fold improvement in the three engineering rounds (i.e. single, doubles, and one MLDE round).

While MULTI-evolve demonstrates broad applicability, its performance depends on identifying a sufficient set of function-enhancing single mutations. In cases where computational approaches, such as PLM zero-shot prediction, fail to predict beneficial mutations and experimental functional data is unavailable, alternative discovery methods would be required. These methods could include phylogenetic approaches (such as ancestral sequence reconstruction or coevolution analysis), structure-based rational design, few-shot learning frameworks, or separate deep learning models trained to identify residues that can improve binding interfaces in antibody-antigen or protein-ligand complexes (56–58). Alternatively, PLM-based prediction can be enhanced through multimodal context, incorporating sequence, structure, and function, or by fine-tuning on functional data, which is becoming feasible as more large-scale functional protein datasets are released (59–62). However, for situations where MULTI-evolve is unable to escape a local maxima in the functional landscape despite identifying function-enhancing mutations, alternative strategies will be required. Looking forward, integrating protein language model embeddings into the MULTI-evolve architecture offers a promising avenue to expand its capabilities (44). In this study, we used one-hot encodings for the MULTI-evolve model, which restricts learning to the specific mutations experimentally characterized in the training set. In contrast, PLM embeddings encode generalized protein features, such as those related to residue-residue contacts and protein folds (27, 28, 63), which could enable MULTI-evolve to learn relationships between protein structure and function that extend beyond the training data. Furthermore, computational oracles that can predict antibody-antigen or protein-ligand interactions (or other desired properties such as solubility or immunogenicity) could be incorporated into an ensemble score that enables MULTI-evolve to consider additional functional information (64, 65). These improvements will further enhance the navigation of complex multi-objective landscapes, where the framework’s data-efficient training allows readout of additional distinct properties. We anticipate MULTI-evolve and other ongoing advances in protein design will enable highly diversified and hyperfunctional proteins across biological research, biotechnology, and therapeutic development.
